{{< include /_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}
{{< include /_webr-options.qmd >}}

All examples on this site share one running story: a QC lab receives a batch of
**ibuprofen 400 mg tablets** and works through four classic experiments —
weigh the tablets, dissolve them, titrate the extracted drug, and build a UV
calibration curve.

The files follow a simple design rule: **one defect per file**. Four datasets
are clean, and each "messy" variant reuses one of them with exactly one
realistic problem, so you learn the data once and then only have to learn the
defect.

Every interactive code cell on this site can load these files directly with
`read_csv("data/...")` — no setup needed. To use a dataset in RStudio, click
its download button and place the file in a `data/` folder inside your R
project.

## Clean datasets

<div class="example-section">
<div class="collapse-toolbar"><button class="collapse-btn">Expand All</button></div>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>tablet_weights.csv</code> — tablet weights off the production line</summary>
<div class="example-body">

24 individual tablets weighed straight off the line, 8 from each of three
batches (A, B, C), with a target weight of about 500 mg. This is the go-to
dataset for inspecting, filtering, grouping, and summarising.

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `tablet_id` | numeric | Tablet number (1–24) |
| `batch` | character | Production batch: `A`, `B`, or `C` |
| `weight_mg` | numeric | Measured tablet weight in milligrams |

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/tablet_weights.csv" download>Download tablet_weights.csv ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

tablet_weights <- read_csv("data/tablet_weights.csv")

tablet_weights
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>dissolution.csv</code> — drug release over time</summary>
<div class="example-body">

Six tablets placed in dissolution fluid, with the percentage of drug released
measured at seven time points per tablet (42 rows). The release climbs toward
100% following first-order kinetics — ideal for plotting curves with
[`ggplot()`](../functions/ggplot.qmd).

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `tablet_id` | numeric | Tablet number (1–6) |
| `time_min` | numeric | Sampling time in minutes |
| `pct_dissolved` | numeric | Percent of the drug released so far |

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/dissolution.csv" download>Download dissolution.csv ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

dissolution <- read_csv("data/dissolution.csv")

dissolution
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>titration.csv</code> — acid–base titration curves</summary>
<div class="example-body">

Acid–base titration of extracted ibuprofen (a weak acid, pKa 4.91) with
0.100 M NaOH. Three replicate samples (A, B, C) are titrated in 2 mL steps,
26 readings each, with equivalence points at 24.5, 25.0, and 25.5 mL.

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `sample_id` | character | Replicate sample: `A`, `B`, or `C` |
| `volume_ml` | numeric | Volume of NaOH added, in mL |
| `pH` | numeric | Measured pH |

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/titration.csv" download>Download titration.csv ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

titration <- read_csv("data/titration.csv")

titration
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>calibration.csv</code> — UV calibration curve</summary>
<div class="example-body">

An ibuprofen UV calibration series following the Beer–Lambert law: absorbance
rises linearly with concentration across 11 standards (R² ≈ 0.9999). This is
the dataset for [`lm()`](../functions/lm.qmd),
[`coef()`](../functions/coef.qmd), and
[`predict()`](../functions/predict.qmd).

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `conc_ug_ml` | numeric | Standard concentration in µg/mL |
| `absorbance` | numeric | Measured UV absorbance |

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/calibration.csv" download>Download calibration.csv ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

calibration <- read_csv("data/calibration.csv")

calibration
```
</div>
</details>

</div>

## Messy variants

Each file below is one of the clean datasets with a single realistic problem
built in. Run the cell to see the problem for yourself — the page for the
matching function shows how to fix it.

<div class="example-section">
<div class="collapse-toolbar"><button class="collapse-btn">Expand All</button></div>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>dissolution_dk.csv</code> — Danish CSV export (semicolons and comma decimals)</summary>
<div class="example-body">

The dissolution data as exported by software with Danish regional settings:
semicolons separate the columns and commas mark the decimals. A plain
`read_csv()` crams everything into one column — this file teaches
[`read_csv2()`](../functions/read-csv.qmd).

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/dissolution_dk.csv" download>Download dissolution_dk.csv ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

read_csv2("data/dissolution_dk.csv")
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>titration_missing.csv</code> — mixed missing-value codes</summary>
<div class="example-body">

The titration data for sample B, but a few pH readings were recorded as
`N/A`, `-`, or simply left blank. Because of the text codes, `read_csv()`
imports the whole `pH` column as text instead of numbers — this file teaches
the [`na =` argument of `read_csv()`](../functions/read-csv.qmd).

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/titration_missing.csv" download>Download titration_missing.csv ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

read_csv("data/titration_missing.csv")
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>weights_units.csv</code> — numbers stored as text</summary>
<div class="example-body">

The tablet weights, but someone typed the unit into every cell
(`"506.3 mg"`). The `weight_mg` column arrives as text, so you can't
calculate with it — this file teaches `parse_number()` and type conversion.

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/weights_units.csv" download>Download weights_units.csv ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

read_csv("data/weights_units.csv")
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>weights_duplicates.csv</code> — rows logged twice</summary>
<div class="example-body">

The tablet weights, but tablets 5 and 18 were accidentally logged twice, so
the file has 26 rows for 24 tablets. Counting the IDs reveals the duplicates
— this file teaches `distinct()`.

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/weights_duplicates.csv" download>Download weights_duplicates.csv ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

weights <- read_csv("data/weights_duplicates.csv")

weights %>% count(tablet_id, sort = TRUE)
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>batches_messy.csv</code> — inconsistent batch labels</summary>
<div class="example-body">

The tablet weights, but the batch column was typed by hand: the same batch
appears as `A`, `a`, `Batch A`, and `" A"` (with a stray space). Grouping or
counting by batch splits one batch into several — this file teaches
`str_trim()` and `str_to_upper()`.

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/batches_messy.csv" download>Download batches_messy.csv ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

batches <- read_csv("data/batches_messy.csv")

batches %>% count(batch)
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>weights_export.csv</code> — instrument export with metadata block</summary>
<div class="example-body">

The tablet weights as a raw balance export: four metadata lines sit above the
header, **and** missing readings use mixed codes (`NA`, `N/A`, `-`, blank).
This is the one deliberate two-defect file, so you can combine
[`skip =` and `na =` in a single `read_csv()` call](../functions/read-csv.qmd).

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/weights_export.csv" download>Download weights_export.csv ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)

read_csv("data/weights_export.csv")
```
</div>
</details>

</div>

## Excel workbooks

<div class="example-section">
<div class="collapse-toolbar"><button class="collapse-btn">Expand All</button></div>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>lab_results.xlsx</code> — all four experiments in one workbook</summary>
<div class="example-body">

One workbook with five sheets: `Weights`, `Dissolution`, `Titration`, and
`Calibration` (the four clean datasets), plus `Weights (missing)` — the
weights with four readings gone, written with mixed NA codes (`N/A`, `-`,
`ND`, blank). It teaches [`read_excel()`](../functions/read-excel.qmd) with
the `sheet =` and `na =` arguments.

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/lab_results.xlsx" download>Download lab_results.xlsx ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(readxl)

excel_sheets("data/lab_results.xlsx")
```

```{webr}
library(readxl)

read_excel("data/lab_results.xlsx", sheet = "Dissolution")
```
</div>
</details>

<details class="example-item">
<summary><code>lab_results_titled.xlsx</code> — title block above the header</summary>
<div class="example-body">

The weights data with a three-row title block above the column names, so the
real header sits on row 4. Reading it naively turns the title into column
names — this file teaches
[`read_excel(skip = 3)`](../functions/read-excel.qmd).

<a class="source-link download-link" href="../data/lab_results_titled.xlsx" download>Download lab_results_titled.xlsx ⬇</a>

```{webr}
library(readxl)

read_excel("data/lab_results_titled.xlsx")
```
</div>
</details>

</div>
